name: Scientific Realism
statement: Our best theories are approximately true, and the unobservable things they posit really exist.
statementAccent: the unobservable things they posit really exist
meaning: Scientific realism is the view that our best, mature scientific theories give us approximately true descriptions of the world, including its unobservable aspects, so that the entities they posit, such as electrons, fields, atoms, and genes, really exist, and science aims at and progressively achieves literally true theories. Realism is usually analyzed as having three commitments. The metaphysical commitment is that there is a mind-independent world for science to describe. The semantic commitment is that the claims of our theories should be read literally, at face value, as truth-apt assertions about that world, including its unobservable parts, rather than as mere instruments for prediction. The epistemic commitment is that we are justified in believing our best theories to be at least approximately true and their central theoretical terms to genuinely refer. The main argument for realism is the no-miracles argument, which holds that the striking predictive and practical success of science would be an inexplicable miracle if its theories were not at least approximately true, so realism is the best explanation of that success. Realism is opposed by anti-realist positions such as instrumentalism and van Fraassen's constructive empiricism, and it is challenged by the underdetermination of theory by evidence and by the pessimistic induction from the history of science.
mechanism: Scientific realism combines a picture of what science describes with an argument for believing it. The picture is that theories are to be taken literally as attempts to describe a mind-independent reality, observable and unobservable alike, and that a good theory is one that is approximately true, its central terms latching onto real features of the world. The chief engine of realism is the no-miracles argument, an inference to the best explanation applied to science as a whole: the sustained predictive and technological success of mature theories, their ability to make novel, precise predictions and to support reliable manipulation of nature, would be a cosmic coincidence, a miracle, unless the theories were at least approximately true and their posited entities real; so approximate truth is the best explanation of success, and we should be realists. Hilary Putnam gave this its famous form, that realism is the only philosophy that does not make the success of science a miracle, and Richard Boyd developed a subtler version grounding the reliability of scientific method in the approximate truth of background theories. Realists then face the anti-realist mechanisms that try to sever success from truth. Constructive empiricism grants a literal reading of theories but withholds belief in their unobservable claims, asking only that they be empirically adequate. Underdetermination and the pessimistic induction argue that empirically equivalent rivals, and the historical record of successful-but-false theories, block the move from success to truth. In response, realists refine their position into selective forms, committing only to the parts of theories, such as their mathematical structure or the constituents essential to novel predictions, that tend to survive theory change.

examples.text: Realism holds there is a mind-independent world, reads theories literally, and believes our best theories approximately true.
Putnam argued that realism is the only philosophy that does not make the success of science a miracle.
The realist takes electrons, fields, and genes to be real entities, not mere useful fictions for predicting observations.

variants.name: Entity realism
variants.text: Hacking and Cartwright's view that we should believe in entities we can manipulate, rather than in whole theories.

variants.name: Structural realism
variants.text: Worrall's view that we should commit only to the mathematical structure of theories, which survives theory change.

whyItMatters: Scientific realism is one of the central debates in the philosophy of science, because it asks what, if anything, the success of science tells us about the world beyond what we can observe. The question matters far beyond philosophy seminars: it bears on whether we should believe in the unobservable entities and structures that modern science posits, from electrons and quarks to genes and spacetime curvature, and on how we understand the achievements and the authority of science. The realist's no-miracles argument gives a powerful expression to the intuition that science's spectacular predictive and technological success would be miraculous unless its theories were getting the world approximately right, an intuition that captures why many scientists take their theories to describe reality. The debate has been remarkably fertile, generating anti-realist alternatives like constructive empiricism and instrumentalism, powerful objections like underdetermination and the pessimistic induction, and sophisticated realist responses like entity realism and structural realism. Each position sharpens our understanding of confirmation, explanation, reference, and the aims of inquiry. As the view that science reveals an approximately true, mind-independent reality including its unobservable depths, scientific realism is a cornerstone question about the meaning of scientific knowledge.

working.text: take scientific claims as truth-apt descriptions of a mind-independent world, including its unobservable parts.
argue, via the no-miracles argument, that approximate truth best explains the success of our theories.
meet underdetermination and the pessimistic induction by committing selectively to structure or to well-tested constituents.

limits: Scientific realism faces two major arguments against it and a family of anti-realist rivals. The underdetermination of theory by evidence urges that empirically equivalent rivals could fit all possible observations, so evidence cannot warrant belief in one theory's particular account of unobservables. The pessimistic induction urges that the history of science is full of successful theories, such as those positing caloric, phlogiston, and the ether, that were later judged false with non-referring terms, so present success is no guarantee of truth. Anti-realists offer alternatives: instrumentalism treats theories as mere tools, and van Fraassen's constructive empiricism accepts theories only as empirically adequate while remaining agnostic about unobservables, arguing that the success of science can be explained without truth, for instance because only successful theories survive. Not all realists even require that theoretical terms genuinely refer, and much turns on the slippery notions of approximate truth and of the observable-unobservable boundary. In reply, realists move to selective positions, entity realism believing only in manipulable entities and structural realism in retained mathematical structure, that concede much to the critics. So scientific realism robustly holds that science approximately describes an unobservable reality, understood as a contested view pressed by underdetermination, the pessimistic induction, and constructive empiricism.
misreadings: Scientific realism does not claim that our best theories are exactly or certainly true, only that they are approximately true and revisable; it is compatible with fallibilism. It is not the trivial claim that the observable world exists, since its distinctive commitment concerns unobservable entities and structures. And it is not defeated merely by noting that theories change, since selective realisms commit only to the parts that survive change, so treating realism as claiming certain exact truth, as being about observables, or as refuted by theory change alone, misreads the position.
origin: The view that our best mature scientific theories are approximately true descriptions of a mind-independent world including its unobservable entities, argued for by the no-miracles argument and opposed by instrumentalism, constructive empiricism, underdetermination, and the pessimistic induction.
